analysis.one_liner: Let Medicare negotiate drug prices like the VA and give beneficiaries the government's bulk-buy rates.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its committee referral and expired when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have let every Medicare beneficiary buy prescription drugs at Federal Supply Schedule prices — the discounted rates the government already pays as a bulk buyer through agencies like the Veterans Administration. It would also repeal the 'non-interference' rule that barred the Health and Human Services Secretary from negotiating drug prices with manufacturers, instead giving the Secretary negotiation authority similar to what the VA and Defense Department have. It died without a hearing, a vote, or even a single cosponsor.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries — more than 40 million people at the time — who would pay Federal Supply Schedule prices for prescriptions, typically well below retail. The bill's stated purpose was to make sure people in drug plans and Medicare Advantage plans 'pay the lowest possible price' [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Any person eligible under Medicare Part A or enrolled under Part B would be entitled to obtain prescription drugs at Federal Supply Schedule prices, the government's bulk-purchase rates [S3].

The bill repeals the Medicare Part D 'non-interference' provision that prohibits the Secretary of Health and Human Services from interfering in negotiations between manufacturers, pharmacies, and drug plan sponsors, or from requiring a formulary price structure [S2].

It instead gives the Secretary authority similar to that of the VA Secretary, the Defense Secretary, and other federal agencies that buy drugs in bulk, to negotiate contracts with manufacturers — with the stated purpose of ensuring beneficiaries pay the lowest possible price [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, who would face a government buyer with VA-style negotiating power over Medicare Part D drugs, and secondarily drug plans and Medicare Advantage plans whose pricing role would shrink [S2]. Taxpayers could also benefit through lower federal drug spending.

drawbacks.text: The bill does not specify how negotiated prices would be enforced, how it would interact with the newly launched Part D private-plan structure, or what happens if manufacturers refuse to negotiate — leaving real implementation questions unanswered in the short two-page text [S3].

The pharmaceutical industry's standard objection to government negotiation is that price controls could reduce revenues and, over time, discourage investment in new medicines; opponents in 2005 also argued that the private-plan competition created by the new Part D program was already lowering costs. This bill would have replaced that market structure with direct government negotiation, a fundamental redesign enacted just two years earlier.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The direct benefit to beneficiaries is straightforward: access to the government's existing bulk-purchase prices, which are routinely lower than retail. The main cost falls on drug manufacturers rather than consumers. The main honest uncertainty is design: the bill is short and does not spell out enforcement mechanics, and it arrived just as the new Part D program launched, so the disruption to that nascent structure would have been significant. On balance the provisions point toward lower out-of-pocket drug costs for Medicare beneficiaries.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bart Stupak introduced H.R. 4610 on December 16, 2005, near the end of the first session of the 109th Congress [S1].
The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and, in addition, to the Ways and Means Committee; it received no further action [S5].
The 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007, and the bill died in committee without a vote [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers are better off, because the 'non-interference' provision barring Medicare from negotiating drug prices remained in effect for more than a decade after this bill died. Medicare beneficiaries who might have paid Federal Supply Schedule prices are worse off.

for.name: Rep. Bart Stupak
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to give Medicare beneficiaries Federal Supply Schedule drug prices and give the HHS Secretary VA-style negotiation authority.

against.name: House committee leadership
against.role: Chairs of the Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce Committees
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; it received no hearing, markup, or floor vote in either committee.

against.name: Pharmaceutical industry
against.role: Brand-name drug manufacturers and their trade groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed government price negotiation for Medicare throughout this period, defending the non-interference provision enacted with the 2003 Part D law.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the bill was introduced by one Democrat, drew no cosponsors from either party, and died in committee.

industries.note: The bill would have given the government VA-style authority to negotiate prices for Part D drugs and repeal the non-interference rule that keeps Medicare out of price talks — directly threatening the industry's pricing power in its largest payer market. Its failure left that pricing power intact [S2].

industries.industry: Prescription drug plan sponsors and Medicare Advantage plans
industries.note: The bill repeals the non-interference clause that protects the private-plan negotiation structure created by Part D, and lets beneficiaries obtain Federal Supply Schedule prices directly — reducing the plans' gatekeeper role in drug pricing [S2].
